corrections.change: (the SameSite rules in lesson 3) → (the later SameSite cookie unit)

The cache only helps when a later request matches the same origin, URL, credentials mode and method/header permissions; a different method or header needs a new preflight. → Reuse requires a matching network partition key, serialized request origin and URL, plus the needed method/header permissions. A credentials-enabled entry can cover a later request without credentials mode include; an entry created without include cannot cover a later include request. A changed method or header needs another preflight only if the cached permissions do not already cover it.

The `SameSite` cookie attribute tells the browser not to send a cookie on **cross-site** requests. → The `SameSite` cookie attribute controls which **cross-site** request contexts permit a cookie; None, Lax and Strict impose different restrictions.

The part of a URL before the colon, such as https, http, mailto or javascript. It says how to interpret the rest of the URL, and it is one of the three parts of an origin. → The part of a URL before its first colon, such as https, mailto or javascript, selecting how the URL is interpreted. Scheme is part of an ordinary HTTP(S) origin; other URL schemes can have opaque or scheme-specific origin rules.

A setting after a cookie's name=value in Set-Cookie. Domain and Path set the cookie's scope (which hosts and URL paths receive it); Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite limit how it is sent and read. Path=/ means every path on the host. → An attribute following a cookie’s name and value in Set-Cookie. Domain and Path affect which requests match, while Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite impose further conditions. Domain scope and path matching do not provide the same isolation as web origins.

One login at an identity provider that gives access to many applications. Its login flows often bounce the browser between sites with cross-site POSTs, which is why Chrome added the Lax+POST exception. → Single sign-on: using an identity-provider authentication flow to access multiple applications. Some deployments involve cross-site POST navigations, one compatibility concern motivating Chromium’s recent-cookie default-SameSite exception.

An HTTP request token expressing semantics such as GET, POST or DELETE. Standard safe methods do not request user-visible state changes; unsafe semantics require an appropriate authorisation and CSRF threat model. A verb alone does not prove an implementation follows those semantics. → An HTTP request token expressing semantics such as GET, POST or DELETE. Safe semantics do not ask for application state changes, although incidental effects such as logging are allowed. Method names do not prove an implementation follows those semantics or enforces authorisation.

The three-digit number at the start of an HTTP response saying how the request went. 200 OK means success, 204 No Content means success with no body (common for preflights) and 403 Forbidden means the server refused. → A three-digit status code associated with an HTTP response. In HTTP/1.1 it appears in a textual status line; newer HTTP versions encode status differently. 200 denotes success, 204 success without content, and 403 refusal to fulfil the request.

A text code that makes the browser show a special character instead of treating it as markup: < for <, > for >, & for &, and " or ' for quotes. → A character reference in HTML source, such as < for a less-than sign or ' for an apostrophe. Interpretation depends on the HTML parsing context: ordinary text and quoted attributes process these references, while script raw-text handling differs.

Writing a character in a URL as % followed by its byte value in hexadecimal, such as %20 for a space or %3C for <. It is the right encoding for URL parts, not for HTML. → Representing a byte as a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits. Text may encode one character into several bytes, commonly UTF-8, before percent-encoding them. Correct handling depends on the URL component and is different from HTML escaping.

A DOM property that sets an element's content as plain text, never parsing it as HTML. The safe replacement for innerHTML when you only need text. → A DOM property replacing an element’s content with plain text instead of parsing HTML markup. Use it for text in an ordinary display element such as a paragraph. Script and style elements have active text semantics, so assigning attacker-controlled text to any element is not universally safe.

Python's function for splitting a URL into scheme, host, path and so on. It only parses; it does not decide whether a URL is safe or match browser parsing exactly. → The urllib.parse.urlparse function splits a URL reference into components; urllib.parse is the containing Python module. Parsing alone does not validate safety or exactly reproduce browser URL interpretation.

A URL without a scheme and host, such as /app.js, resolved against the page's base URL. → A URL reference resolved against a base URL. It may omit both scheme and host, as /app.js does, or include an authority while omitting the scheme, as //cdn.example/app.js does. Validate the parsed destination rather than assuming every relative reference stays on the original host.

A CSP source keyword meaning the page's own origin. → A CSP source keyword matching the protected resource’s origin under CSP’s specific scheme, host and port rules. The matching rules can permit secure-scheme upgrades; it is not a universal raw-string origin comparison.

A random number generator whose output an attacker cannot predict, even after seeing earlier outputs. Python's secrets module uses one; tokens and nonces must come from one. → A generator designed to make feasible observations give negligible computational predictive advantage, under assumptions about its seed and implementation. State compromise needs separate analysis. Python secrets uses operating-system cryptographic randomness; nonce requirements still depend on the protocol.

The smallest unit of information: a single 0 or 1. A random value of n bits has 2^n possible values, so each extra bit doubles the guessing work. → A binary digit with two values, zero and one. Uniformly choosing n independent bits yields a space of two to the n possible strings; merely storing n bits does not ensure that much unpredictable entropy.
non-ASCII alias for ASCII → Removed opposite-sense alias; distinct Non-ASCII entry added.

Session data stored in the cookie itself and signed by the server so it cannot be altered, as Flask does by default. The user can still read it, and the server keeps no copy. → Session data carried in a client cookie and authenticated by a server-held signing key, as in Flask’s default session implementation. Signing detects unauthorised changes under the scheme’s bounds but does not hide the data. Whether the application retains other server-side state is a separate design choice.

The part of a URL after #, which page script reads through location.hash. Browsers do not include it in the HTTP request, so the server never sees it unless page script sends it on. That is why server-side defences miss DOM XSS that starts there. → The part of a URL after its fragment marker, exposed to page script through location.hash. It is excluded from an ordinary HTTP request target; client code can transmit it separately. Server response escaping alone does not transform a fragment on an independent client-side DOM path.

The cookie attribute that hides the cookie from page script such as document.cookie, so injected script cannot read and steal it. The browser still attaches it to requests, so XSS can still act as the user. → A cookie attribute preventing direct access through non-HTTP APIs such as document.cookie. Eligible cookies can still accompany requests made by injected same-origin script, so HttpOnly does not prevent all session abuse or theft paths.

A SameSite value that withholds the cookie on every cross-site request, including clicking a link from another site. Safest, but a user arriving from a link can look logged out on the first page. → A SameSite value withholding the cookie on cross-site requests, including an initial navigation from a cross-site link. It is the most restrictive SameSite setting; the initial request can therefore appear unauthenticated when that cookie is the only session credential.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, meaning any origin may read the response. Browsers refuse it for credentialed requests, so a response tied to a user's cookies must name an exact origin. → Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * permits response sharing when the request’s credentials mode is not include. Mode include requires an explicit matching origin, even if no cookie was actually sent. Other browser and server checks still apply.

A non-standard request header that page script adds, such as X-Requested-With. It is not CORS-safelisted, so a cross-origin page can only send it after a preflight the server approves; requiring one blocks simple-request CSRF. → An application-defined request field such as X-Requested-With. A cross-origin CORS request using a non-safelisted author-set header needs preflight permission, which can be cached. Requiring that field helps only with strict validation, restrictive CORS and no accepted ambient-authentication bypass.

A URL starting javascript: that runs the rest as code when followed. It contains no special HTML characters, so escaping does not stop it; URL attributes need a scheme allowlist. → A URL using the javascript scheme to request script evaluation when the relevant navigation and browser policies permit it. HTML escaping does not validate this URL scheme; apply destination-appropriate URL validation and output encoding.

A security professional paid to attack a system, with permission, to find vulnerabilities before real attackers do. That authorised attack is called a penetration test (pen test). → A person conducting an authorised security assessment that attempts to find and demonstrate weaknesses within an agreed scope. It can be an internal or external role; being paid is not part of the technical definition.
It parses it as markup and runs it. → Without an independent execution restriction such as CSP, it parses the value as markup and can run the script.

gaps: No complete browser/version compatibility matrix or long real preflight-retention measurement.
Recent-cookie 120-second default-mode behavior is checked against Chromium guidance/source and arithmetic; no two-minute cookie-aging browser experiment is claimed.
Partial Flask, CSP, message and Trusted Types examples need the stated setup and production integration; passing local fixtures do not prove full application security.
Samy and Google’s sampled CSP study are historical source-backed cases; their spread or coverage is not newly reproduced.
